noteRef.topicTitle: The nature and variety of living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the term pathogen and know that pathogens may include fungi, bacteria, protoctists or viruses Viruses: these are not living organisms. They are small particles, smaller than bacteria; they are parasitic and can reproduce only inside living cells; they infect every type of living organism. They have a wide variety of shapes and sizes; they have no cellular structure but have a protein coat and contain one type of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA. Examples include the tobacco mosaic virus that causes discolouring of the leaves of tobacco plants by preventing the formation of chloroplasts, the influenza virus that causes ‘flu’ and the HIV virus that causes AIDS.

primer.text: A pathogen is any organism that brings about disease inside a different organism, but the label stretches across several groups. This note walks the cellular pathogens first — bacteria, fungi and protoctists — then the viruses, which are not living organisms at all, and finishes with the three named examples: tobacco mosaic virus, HIV and influenza.

lessons.title: Cellular pathogens: bacteria, fungi and protoctists
lessons.opening: The disease-causing club is not a single family: bacteria, fungi and protoctists all contribute members, and viruses join them despite not being alive. Each group attacks differently — bacteria may stay in body spaces instead of invading cells, fungi favour plant hosts, and one protoctist, Plasmodium falciparum, spreads malaria through mosquito bites.
keyPoints: A pathogen is defined as any organism that brings about disease inside a different organism.
Pathogenic bacteria can remain in body cavities or spaces rather than infecting host cells.
Pneumococcus is the named bacterium behind pneumonia; some Mucor species are plant pathogens.
Plasmodium falciparum is the protoctist that causes severe malaria and travels by mosquito.

low.restatement: Pathogens cause disease. Bacteria, fungi and protoctists all include pathogenic members; Pneumococcus, Mucor and Plasmodium are the named examples.
low.analogy: Think of pathogens as three different families of unwelcome guests, each with its own way of getting through the door.
low.examPointer: Match each named example to its group and disease — that pairing is what 'know that pathogens may include...' questions reward.

medium.restatement: Pathogenicity cuts across classification: the cellular groups contribute members with distinct infection styles, from surface-dwelling bacteria to mosquito-borne protoctist parasites.
medium.analogy: Being dangerous is a job title, not a family name — members of very different households can hold the same job.
medium.examPointer: Marks are lost by claiming ALL members of a group are pathogenic — the note says 'some' Mucor species and single named examples.

check.stem: Which definition matches the term pathogen?

options.text: An organism that brings about disease inside a different organism
options.explanation: This matches the note's definition.

options.text: Any microscopic particle found in the air
options.explanation: Pathogens are organisms causing disease, not any particle.

options.text: Any organism living inside a host
options.explanation: Many internal organisms are harmless; causing disease is the deciding property.

options.text: Any organism that feeds on dead material
options.explanation: Decomposer feeding is not disease-causing.

check.stem: Which group of organisms includes pathogens but is NOT classified among living organisms?

options.text: Protoctists
options.explanation: Protoctists are living eukaryotes.

options.text: Viruses
options.explanation: Viruses cause disease yet sit outside the classification of living organisms.

options.text: Bacteria
options.explanation: Bacteria are living prokaryotes.

options.text: Fungi
options.explanation: Fungi are living eukaryotes.

check.stem: How do pathogenic bacteria such as Pneumococcus sometimes behave, according to the note?

options.text: They only infect plants
options.explanation: Pneumonia is a human disease.

options.text: They are always harmless
options.explanation: They cause pneumonia.

options.text: They can stay within body cavities or spaces without infecting host cells
options.explanation: The note states they do not always infect host cells.

options.text: They always invade and take over host cells
options.explanation: That describes viruses, not these bacteria.

check.stem: Which pairing of pathogen example and disease is correct?

options.text: Pneumococcus — malaria
options.explanation: Pneumococcus causes pneumonia.

options.text: Mucor — malaria in humans
options.explanation: Mucor is a plant-infecting fungus.

options.text: TMV — malaria
options.explanation: TMV is a plant virus.

options.text: Plasmodium falciparum — malaria spread by mosquitoes
options.explanation: The named protoctist and its vector pair correctly.

check.stem: Why is 'all fungi are pathogens' a wrong claim to write in an exam?

options.text: Because only some Mucor species are pathogenic and most fungi are harmless decomposers or food makers
options.explanation: The note deliberately says some (but not all) Mucor species are pathogenic.

options.text: Because fungi are prokaryotes and cannot infect anything
options.explanation: Fungi are eukaryotes and some do infect.

options.text: Because fungi lack cell walls
options.explanation: Fungi have walls.

options.text: Because pathogens must be single-celled
options.explanation: Multicellular fungi can be pathogenic.

check.stem: Give the term for an organism that brings about disease in a different organism.
Name the protoctist pathogen and the disease it causes.
Explain why the three named cellular pathogen groups can look so different from one another yet still share the pathogen label.
check.modelAnswer: The label describes what an organism does — causing disease in a host — not how it is built, so a wall-carrying bacterium, a hyphal fungus and a parasite protoctist can all qualify despite sitting in three different classification groups.

check.stem: A gardener finds a plant with discoloured, wilting leaves and suspects three culprits: a bacterium, a fungus and a virus. Using this note's examples, name one named species for two of the culprit classes.
check.modelAnswer: A fungal culprit could be a Mucor species (some are plant pathogens) and a viral culprit could be tobacco mosaic virus; the bacterium slot would need a plant-infecting bacterial species rather than the human-lung Pneumococcus.

lessons.title: Viruses: structure, behaviour and the three named cases
lessons.opening: Viruses occupy a strange corner of biology: they carry a protein coat and one type of nucleic acid, yet they perform none of the eight life processes for themselves. They reproduce only inside living cells and infect every type of living organism. Tobacco mosaic virus, HIV and the influenza virus are the three cases to know.
keyPoints: Viruses are particles smaller than bacteria with no cellular structure: a protein coat around one type of nucleic acid.
Viruses can reproduce only inside living host cells, which they take over.
Tobacco mosaic virus discolours tobacco leaves by damaging chloroplast formation and cuts crop yield.
HIV attacks immune-system cells and can progress to AIDS; influenza causes flu in humans.

low.restatement: A virus is a small particle: protein coat plus DNA or RNA. It reproduces only inside living cells; TMV hits plants, HIV leads to AIDS, influenza causes flu.
low.analogy: A virus is a recipe card in a protective sleeve — inert on the shelf, but it hijacks a kitchen (the host cell) to cook copies of itself.
low.examPointer: Write 'not considered living' explicitly when comparing viruses with cellular pathogens — it is the fact examiners look for.

medium.restatement: The non-living status follows from the absence of independent life processes; host takeover supplies reproduction, and each named virus is defined by its host and its disease.
medium.analogy: Viruses are parasites of machinery rather than of meals: they bring no factory, only instructions the factory is forced to run.
medium.examPointer: For HIV, note the delay — hidden in the immune system for years — before AIDS; the timeline detail separates strong answers.

check.stem: What does a virus particle contain?

options.text: A protein coat around one type of nucleic acid
options.explanation: This matches the note's structure description.

options.text: A cell wall, membrane and cytoplasm
options.explanation: Viruses have no cellular structure.

options.text: Mitochondria and ribosomes
options.explanation: Viruses carry no organelles.

options.text: Many types of nucleic acid and a nucleus
options.explanation: One nucleic acid type and no nucleus.

check.stem: Why are viruses excluded from the classification of living organisms?

options.text: Because they lack nucleic acid
options.explanation: Every virus carries DNA or RNA.

options.text: Because they perform none of the eight life processes on their own
options.explanation: The note gives exactly this reason.

options.text: Because they are too small to see with a microscope
options.explanation: Smallness is not the exclusion reason.

options.text: Because they cannot cause disease
options.explanation: Causing disease is what they do best.

check.stem: Which statement about virus reproduction is correct?

options.text: Viruses reproduce by cell division
options.explanation: Viruses have no cells to divide.

options.text: Viruses never reproduce at all
options.explanation: They reproduce via host cells.

options.text: Viruses can reproduce only inside living host cells
options.explanation: Parasitic reproduction inside living cells is the named rule.

options.text: Viruses reproduce freely in soil and water
options.explanation: They need living cells.

check.stem: A tobacco plant shows a mosaic pattern of leaf discolouration and poor growth. Which pathogen fits, and what is the mechanism?

options.text: Plasmodium falciparum, which destroys red blood cells
options.explanation: That is the malaria protoctist of humans.

options.text: Pneumococcus, which infects the lungs
options.explanation: That is a human lung pathogen.

options.text: A Mucor fungus, which rots the roots
options.explanation: The mosaic pattern is TMV's signature.

options.text: Tobacco mosaic virus, which damages chloroplast formation and so reduces photosynthesis
options.explanation: The note ties the discolouration to chloroplast damage and the poor growth to reduced photosynthesis.

check.stem: Which description of HIV's course through the immune system matches the note?

options.text: It begins flu-like, hides in the immune system for years, and can end in AIDS
options.explanation: The three-stage course is the note's account.

options.text: It kills within days of infection
options.explanation: The note describes years of hidden presence.

options.text: It never damages the immune system
options.explanation: Immune damage is its defining effect.

options.text: It is spread only through the air
options.explanation: The named routes are sexual contact and bodily-fluid exchange.

check.stem: State the two components that make up every virus particle.
check.modelAnswer: A protein coat and one type of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA).

check.stem: Name the virus that causes flu in humans.
Explain why a virus needs a host cell even though it carries its own genetic instructions.
check.modelAnswer: A virus owns instructions but no machinery: with no cytoplasm, organelles or metabolism, it cannot run the eight life processes alone, so it must take over a host cell's metabolic equipment to build new virus particles.

check.stem: A lab notebook lists three isolates: one taken from diseased tobacco leaves, one from a patient's immune cells, and one from an airway lining sample. Assign the likely virus to each sample.
check.modelAnswer: Leaf isolate: tobacco mosaic virus; immune-cell isolate: HIV; airway lining isolate: influenza virus — each virus matches the tissue its disease targets.

glossary.definition: An organism that brings about disease inside a different organism.
The information-carrying molecule (DNA or RNA) found inside a virus particle.
The outer protective layer of a virus particle.
